row.question_original: My child is in early elementary school and learning to read. Should we try SpellRead to help my child understand what they read?

replies:
SpellRead can help, but it depends on why your child is struggling to understand what they read.

SpellRead is a structured literacy program that teaches reading explicitly and systematically: sounds, letter patterns, decoding, spelling, and fluency. It's often used for children who struggle with word reading, including those with dyslexia. Comprehension builds on accurate, effortless word reading, so for a child who is stumbling over words, a program like this can make a real difference. But it mainly targets decoding. It doesn't directly teach comprehension, and a child who reads words well can still struggle to understand text.

To figure out what your child needs, consider a few questions:

- **Can your child read the words accurately?** If they sound out words slowly, guess based on the first letter, or read in a choppy way, decoding is probably the bottleneck, and SpellRead would be a good fit.
- **Can your child understand the same material when someone reads it aloud?** If so, their decoding is the main issue. If not, the problem is more likely vocabulary, background knowledge, or language skills, and those need attention too.
- **What does the teacher see?** Ask for a reading assessment that separates word reading from comprehension. Many schools can provide this, and it will show where the gap is.

Whatever the cause, reading aloud to your child every day, talking about books, building vocabulary through conversation, and asking questions like "What do you think will happen next?" or "Why did she do that?" all support comprehension.

If you do try SpellRead, it works best with trained instructors, usually in short, frequent sessions. Ask your school whether they offer it or can recommend a certified tutor. Progress is typically measured over months, so give it a fair trial and check in regularly with the teacher.

The strength of the evidence varies a lot across the claims I made.

**Strong evidence:**
- **The Simple View of Reading** (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Hoover & Gough, 1990) is one of the most replicated frameworks in reading research. It holds that reading comprehension depends on both word-reading accuracy and language comprehension (vocabulary, background knowledge, grammar). This is the basis for my point that comprehension problems can come from decoding, language, or both, and for the suggestion to test whether your child understands material read aloud.
- **Explicit, systematic phonics** is well supported. The National Reading Panel (2000) and later meta-analyses found it improves word reading, especially in early grades.

**Moderate or weaker evidence:**
- **Orton-Gillingham-based programs**, which SpellRead draws on, have a substantial clinical following, but the research is thinner. Reviews have found mostly small studies, many with weak designs, and mixed results. Some find benefits, but the evidence doesn't establish that they are superior to other structured literacy approaches.
- **SpellRead specifically:** I don't have reliable detail on its independent research. I believe there are some studies, but I can't confidently describe their quality, sample sizes, or whether they were conducted independently of the publisher. I should have been more careful in my first answer when I said it "can make a real difference." That was a reasonable expectation based on the approach, not a verified finding about this program.

**How to check:**
- Search the **What Works Clearinghouse** (ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc) and **Evidence for ESSA** (evidenceforessa.org), which review reading programs against consistent standards. If SpellRead has been reviewed, you'll see the findings directly.
- Ask the publisher for its published studies, and check whether they are peer-reviewed and independent.
- Ask your child's teacher or a reading specialist what they've seen work locally.

The most solid part of my earlier advice is the distinction between decoding and comprehension, and the value of a diagnostic assessment to find which one your child needs.

IT DEPENDS. Whether SpellRead is right for your child depends on whether they struggle to decode words. If they sound out words slowly, guess from the first letter, or read choppily, a structured decoding program is likely worth trying. If they read words accurately but don't understand what they read, the main need is probably vocabulary, background knowledge, or language skills, and SpellRead would address only part of that.

I also need to correct my last answer. I said the What Works Clearinghouse found positive effects for SpellRead across several large studies, but I can't verify that, and I shouldn't have stated it as established. Structured literacy approaches as a whole have solid research support, but the evidence for this specific program is less clear than I implied.

Before deciding, ask the teacher or a reading specialist for an assessment that separates word reading from comprehension. Their results will tell you which kind of help your child needs. You can also check the What Works Clearinghouse website (ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc) directly to see what it has rated for SpellRead.
